extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, inventors, and legal historians interested in English patent and monopoly law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of English law governing monopolies and patents for inventions: historical background, common-law principles, statutory constraints (notably 21 Jac. I), and offences in domestic trade (forestalling, engrossing, regrating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / new invention requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: At common law the King could grant a patent to any person who, at his own charge, or by his own industry, wit, or invention, had introduced any new and profitable trade into the realm, or any engine that had never before been used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is a necessary incident to the thing over which an exclusive power was to be given by the patent. Examples: grants were declared void where the claimed subject-matter had been previously used or made public (cases cited: Hastings, Matthews, the seive case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public disclosure defeats patent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is void if, in addition to the patentee's discovery, it claims the discovery of something already made public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the sail-cloth case: patent for making sail cloth 'without any starch whatever' was void because exclusion of starch had been discovered and made public before (Cawpin v. Denyon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trivial differences insufficient for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight differences from earlier known goods or techniques do not sustain a patent if the core invention or method was already practiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Matthews the cutler; Hastings the frisadoes maker) show patents supported until it appeared others had made similar goods with only slight differences; courts then declared the grants void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents must not restrain lawful trade (monopoly prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any royal grant, licence, or allowance that restrains persons of liberties they previously had, or hinders them in their lawful trade, is a monopoly and void at common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of grants held void: sole engrossing of wills and inventories in spiritual courts; sole making of bills, pleas and writs in courts of law; sole making/importing/selling of playing cards; charters conferring exclusive importation or trading rights that debarr others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of grants (analysis for treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent and grants may be considered under three heads: (1) grants valid at common law, (2) those bad at common law, and (3) those permitted by statute law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy structures legal analysis: first examine common-law-valid grants, then void ones, then statute-authorized exceptions (e.g., patents under 21 Jac. I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants valid at common law (scope and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: At common law the King could make a patent to continue for a reasonable time for someone who introduced a new and profitable trade or a new engine tending to the furtherance of trade, thereby allowing the grantee to confine use to himself and enjoy the benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such grants were meant to reward introduction/importation of useful arts (examples: bringing methods from abroad). The grant was valid unless shown that the method or trade was already practiced in the realm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory declaration permitting patents for new inventions (21 Jac. I)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute 21 Jac. I (c.3) declared monopolies void generally but inserted a clause permitting the Sovereign to grant patents for new inventions, provided they do not endure for more than fourteen years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory clause is the foundation of patent law: it limits both subject-matter (new inventions only) and duration (max 14 years). The Treatise treats the second Book as commentary on that clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal limit of patents (fourteen years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents granted under the statute are permitted only provided they are not made to endure for a longer time than fourteen years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 14-year cap is explicit in the statute (21 Jac. I s.6) and is presented as a mandatory temporal constraint on exclusive privileges granted by the Crown/legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary role for creating new monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is in contemplation to constitute a new monopoly beyond individual patents, recourse must be had to Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory monopolies (e.g., charters like the East India Company or trade confinements) arise only through legislative action rather than prerogative; statutes have been used to increase inventors' benefits by extending duration or enlarging interested persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: King's limited discretion to grant exclusive employments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is considered that the King may grant to particular persons the sole use of some particular employments (as of printing the Holy Scriptures, and law books, etc.) in the exercise of which an unrestrained liberty might be of dangerous consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such grants are treated as exceptions justified by public interest or necessity, but the extent and limits of this rule are to be examined (the Treatise flags further discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolies by individuals — forestalling, engrossing, regrating
rubrics_metrics.description: Private monopolistic offences in domestic trade consist of forestalling (buying goods before they reach market or dissuading sellers), engrossing (buying/hoarding large quantities to artificially raise prices), and regrating (buying and reselling victuals in market to enhance price).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These acts are actionable at common law and have been the subject of many statutes; the Treatise outlines definitions, the nature of each offence, what things they may be committed in, and proceedings to punish offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory regime and historic statutes addressing domestic monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous historic statutes regulate forestalling, engrossing, and regrating (examples: 51 Hen. III stat. 6 c.1; ordinances of Edward I; 25 Edward III; 5 & 6 Edward VI; statutes concerning assize of bread, regulations of buying cattle, limits on sheep holdings, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Treatise notes many statutes are unrepealed, some repealed (e.g., by 12 Geo. III c.71), and that statutes often merely declared the common law; it also records penalties (pillory, forfeiture, etc.) and that practice has rendered some statutes obsolete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy and invalidation where grant encroaches on public liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants that trench upon acknowledged privileges of members of society or that create exclusive rights in ordinary trades will be held void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical judicial reasoning (e.g., Darcy's Case) emphasizes that patents which effectively take away a man's skill or livelihood discourage labour and are contrary to public policy; courts have invalidated such grants to preserve freedom of trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between monopoly and engrossing (source and remedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopoly (exclusive grant) typically arises from a patent or royal grant, whereas engrossing is an act of subjects in trade which creates scarcity and may be punished under statutes or common-law offence frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Treatise signals that though both restrict supply, their legal treatment, sources, and corrective measures differ; readers uninterested in domestic monopolies may skip the chapter, as it is separate from patent law for inventions.
